Neonates of the Ruddy turnstone (Arenaria interpres) emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after an incubation period of approximately 21.9 days [ab = approximately 21.9 days]. At this stage, hatchlings exhibit a modest body mass, with the wet weight at birth recorded at 11.5 grams [Wwb = 11.5 grams], a value consistent with the semi-precocial developmental mode of this migratory shorebird. The initial wet weight of the newly hatched chick, however, is somewhat higher at 17.9 grams [Ww0 = 17.9 grams], reflecting the residual mass of the yolk sac that is internalized prior to emergence. This initial weight provides a crucial energy reserve during the first few days of life, when the altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental brooding and the thermoregulatory stability provided by the nest environment at the recorded incubation temperature. The yolk reserves are rapidly metabolized to support early growth and thermogenesis, enabling the young bird to transition to exogenous feeding within a short window following hatching.

Under field conditions typical of the Arctic and subarctic breeding grounds, where ambient temperatures can be cold, the body temperature of active Ruddy turnstone adults is regulated at approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. At this thermal regime, the developmental timeline is tightly constrained by the short Arctic summer. Fledging occurs rapidly at 22 days since birth [tx = 22 days since birth], a period that is critical for the young to gain independence before the fall migration southward at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This brief nestling phase is followed by a longer juvenile period, during which the bird must acquire foraging skills and accumulate sufficient fat reserves for the long migratory journey. The sexual maturation process, leading to the initiation of gonadal activity, does not occur during the first year of life. Instead, puberty is attained at 66 days since birth [tp = 66 days since birth], which is surprisingly early, though this likely represents the initiation of hormonal development rather than functional reproductive capability at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This early onset of gonadal development is an adaptation to the brief breeding window available in polar regions.

The ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, in Ruddy turnstone is a sexually dimorphic trait. Adult females, which are typically larger than males, attain an ultimate wet weight of 113 grams [Wwi = 113 grams], a measurement that reflects the energetic demands of egg production and incubation duties. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight of male Ruddy turnstones is slightly lower at 108 grams [Wwi = 108 grams], a difference that is consistent with sexual size dimorphism observed across many Charadriiformes. These mass values are indicative of a robust, stocky shorebird adapted to a demanding lifestyle of long-distance migration and benthic foraging along intertidal shores. The relatively heavy body mass for a bird of this size facilitates endurance during sustained flight and provides thermal inertia during cold exposure. Intraspecific variation in these weights can be observed depending on the timing of measurement, with individuals being heaviest just prior to migration due to hyperphagia and fat deposition. Museum specimen series and field measurements from breeding grounds have consistently demonstrated this size differential.

Under the metabolic conditions typical of active adults, at a stable body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Ruddy turnstone has been documented through long-term banding studies. The maximum recorded longevity reaches approximately 23.8 years [am = approximately 23.8 years], an exceptionally long lifespan for a shorebird of this body size at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This extended longevity is facilitated by a relatively low annual adult mortality rate and the deferred onset of reproduction. At the same thermal regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at first brood, the age at which an individual successfully produces its first clutch, is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days], meaning that most birds do not breed until their second or third calendar year. This delayed reproductive strategy allows young adults to gain foraging experience, establish territories, and develop the physiological condition necessary for successful incubation and chick-rearing. The deferred reproduction is a common life-history tactic among long-lived seabirds and shorebirds, balancing the high survival probability of adults with the uncertain success of their first few breeding attempts. Both field data and life-table analyses support this pattern, indicating that reproductive value peaks in middle age.

Reproductive output in the Ruddy turnstone is characterized by a single clutch per season, a strategy typical of Arctic-nesting shorebirds facing a compressed breeding window. Females produce a clutch of exactly 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch] in a typical nesting attempt. The frequency of these reproductive events is limited to 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], meaning that renesting after a failed attempt is uncommon and often unsuccessful due to time constraints. When the entire annual reproductive output is reconsidered, this amounts to 4 eggs per year [Ri = 4 eggs per year]. This low fecundity is compensated by the high survival rate of adults and the relatively long breeding life of this species, which spans many years. Under optimal conditions at a stable body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the females are capable of producing this single brood reliably, but the success of each brood is highly dependent on the timing of snowmelt and the abundance of invertebrate prey on the tundra. Coastal populations show slightly less temporal constraint but similar clutch parameters.
